title: ‘Show How 3M Is 0% at Fault:’ Expert Witness Used ChatGPT to Write Report Defending Company in Deadly Explosion Lawsuit

reading.body:
This incident shows an expert witness using a general-purpose conversational AI to draft a formal legal report, with prompts explicitly directing the system to reach a predetermined conclusion. That is not how expert analysis is supposed to work: the output was shaped by the instruction rather than by independent evaluation of the evidence. The failure sits at the point where a human professional chose to delegate a judgment task to a tool that simply generates text consistent with whatever goal is stated in the prompt.

The prompts became visible through the discovery process, which is how the use of the tool came to light at all. There was no institutional check, before submission, that would have flagged that the report's reasoning originated in a directive to exonerate a specific party. A standard peer or counsel review of the document itself might not have caught it either, since the output could read as coherent analysis without revealing how it was produced.

What is not established is whether the report's conclusions were factually wrong, whether any court has ruled on the admissibility or weight of the testimony, or whether any party has been found liable in the underlying lawsuit.

reports.title: ‘Show How 3M Is 0% at Fault:’ Expert Witness Used ChatGPT to Write Report Defending Company in Deadly Explosion Lawsuit

summary:
An expert witness hired by 3M to defend the company in a lawsuit used ChatGPT to write significant portions of his expert report. The witness's AI prompts, which became public through court documents, revealed he asked the chatbot to create a report showing that 3M was "0% at fault" for a 2020 explosion at a Houston manufacturing facility. The case involves a $61 million lawsuit stemming from the explosion that killed three people and destroyed approximately 200 homes.

The incident highlights how artificial intelligence is increasingly being used in courtrooms, including in expert witness testimonies. According to court records, the 2020 explosion at Watson Grinding was caused by a degraded and poorly crimped rubber welding hose that leaked flammable gas. Homeowners sued 3M and Watson Grinding, claiming 3M failed to properly service the facility's gas detection system and made other errors contributing to the disaster. The case demonstrates that AI prompts used to generate expert testimony can be discovered during litigation and potentially prove damaging to a defendant's case.
